PUPCET and College Admission

The Polytechnic University of the Philippines College Entrance Test (PUPCET) is the standard admission requirement for incoming freshmen who want to enter a PUP campus, particularly the highly competitive Manila campus. Eligible takers include graduating senior high school students and recent graduates who have not yet enrolled in any college degree, diploma, or technical program. Applicants who have already taken college-level units are generally disqualified from taking the test as a freshman applicant.

Because PUP is a state university with heavily subsidized tuition, demand for slots far exceeds supply - historically only a small fraction of examinees nationwide are admitted to the Manila campus each year. When the standard entrance exam is suspended (as happened during the pandemic years), PUP has used alternative evaluation schemes such as the College Admission Evaluation (CAEPUP), processed through the university's online application portal, iApply.

PUP also grants entrance scholarships to outstanding senior high school graduates who have not enrolled elsewhere and can show strong academic performance, in lieu of or in addition to taking the entrance exam.

Enrollment Procedure for New and Continuing Students

Only students who have completed official enrollment are permitted to attend classes or be marked present in a class roster. New freshmen typically enroll after passing PUPCET or an equivalent admission evaluation, following a sequence of document submission, subject assignment/adviser approval, payment of applicable fees, and confirmation through the university's enrollment system.

Continuing students re-enroll each semester through the same online system, subject to being in good academic standing and having no unresolved holds (e.g., unpaid fees, missing clearance, incomplete grades that have lapsed). Enrollment periods are announced through official PUP channels ahead of each semester, and students are encouraged to enroll early since sections and slots for popular subjects fill up quickly.

Late enrollment is generally discouraged and may require special approval from the college dean's office, especially once regular classes have already started.

Academic Load, Prerequisite and Advanced Subjects

Each degree program prescribes a normal academic load (a set number of units) per semester. As a general rule, a student may not take an advanced subject until the prerequisite subject has been passed. In some cases, a student may be allowed to enroll in a prerequisite and its advanced/co-requisite subject in the same term, but only with the recommendation and approval of the department chairperson or college dean.

Graduating students in their last term may be granted an excess or overload - additional units beyond the normal load - at the discretion of the Vice President for Academic Affairs, typically capped at six (6) additional academic units, so they can complete remaining requirements and graduate on time.

Students who wish to change subjects, substitute a subject, or drop a subject after enrollment must file the appropriate request with their department, which then gets submitted to the Registrar's Office for processing.

Classification of Students

PUP classifies students based on their academic standing and load, such as regular students (those following the prescribed sequence and load per year level) and irregular students (those who are behind or ahead of the standard sequence, often due to failed, dropped, or overloaded subjects). Classification affects a student's priority during enrollment and which sections they are eligible to enroll in.

Detailed classification rules, along with admission policies for shifting between programs or colleges, are maintained by the respective College Dean's Office in coordination with the Office of Admission Services. Students who want to shift programs or transfer colleges should coordinate directly with these offices, as requirements vary by program and are subject to slot availability.

Grading System

PUP uses a numeric grading scale ranging from 1.00 (Excellent, the highest) to 5.00 (Fail). For undergraduate programs, 3.00 is the lowest passing grade; grades between 3.25 and 5.00 are failing. Non-numeric marks are also used for special situations:
INC (Incomplete) - given when a student is otherwise passing but has not completed a major requirement (e.g., a final exam or major project). The requirement must typically be completed within one year from the end of the term; otherwise the INC automatically converts to a failing grade.
W (Withdrawn) - given when a student formally withdraws from a subject in writing, and must be filed no later than one month before the final examination period.
D (Dropped) - given when a faculty member drops a student from the class roll for exceeding the allowed number of absences, or for never having attended the class.

A student who already earned a passing grade in a subject is not allowed to retake the examination solely to improve that grade. Graduate programs apply stricter passing standards than undergraduate programs (e.g., master's and doctoral students must maintain higher minimum weighted averages to remain in good standing).

Attendance Policy

Students are expected to attend all scheduled class sessions. Excused absences (e.g., due to illness or an official university-sanctioned activity) require supporting documentation, and in some cases an excuse slip issued through the Guidance, Counseling and Testing Services Office (GCTSO).

Importantly, an excused absence only excuses the student from being marked absent - it does not excuse them from the coursework. All lessons, activities, quizzes, or requirements covered during the missed session must still be completed by the student within a reasonable period set by the instructor.

Students who accumulate absences beyond the allowable limit for a subject (typically tied to a percentage of total class hours) may be given a Dropped (D) mark by the instructor.

Late Reporting and Correction of Grades

If a grade or mark was recorded incorrectly, the correction must generally be filed and processed within one semester from when the grade was originally received. Requests filed beyond this window may no longer be honored under standard policy, so students who spot a discrepancy on their grade record should report it to their instructor and the Registrar's Office as soon as possible.

Late reporting of grades (i.e., a faculty member submitting a grade past the official deadline) follows a separate university process and is typically routed through the department and Registrar's Office as well.

Removing an Incomplete (INC) Mark

A student who receives an Incomplete (INC) mark must formally request its removal by submitting a Completion Form, along with supporting documents such as the faculty member's class record and the student's registration certificate, to the appropriate university office (typically routed through the college and the Office of the University Registrar).

The outstanding requirement (e.g., a missed major exam) must be completed within one year of the end of the term in which the INC was given. If the deadline lapses without completion, the INC is automatically converted to a failing grade under standard policy, so students are strongly advised not to delay.

Scholarships and Financial Assistance

PUP offers several forms of financial assistance to students, including academic scholarships tied to grade thresholds (commonly requiring a general weighted average around 1.75-2.0 or better, depending on the specific scholarship program), entrance scholarships for outstanding incoming freshmen, and other assistance programs such as student loan funds, book banks, and cultural or student assistantship programs that let students work in exchange for support.

Students interested in applying should coordinate with their college's scholarship coordinator or the university's Scholarship and Financial Assistance Office, since application periods, required documents, and specific GWA cutoffs vary by scholarship type and are announced each semester.

Dean's List and Academic Standing

Students are expected to maintain good academic standing, generally reflected by a General Weighted Average (GWA) of 2.0 or better for undergraduates. Falling consistently below the required standing may result in an academic warning, probation, or in repeated cases, dismissal from the program, depending on specific college and program rules.

Recognition such as the Dean's List is awarded to students who exceed specific GWA thresholds each semester (often in the 1.00-1.75 range depending on the college), along with meeting a minimum unit load and having no failing or incomplete grades in the term being evaluated.

Student ID and Campus Entry Policy

Students are required to carry and present a valid PUP student identification card when entering campus, in line with the university's "No ID, No Entry" policy. However, a student who does not have their ID on hand should not automatically be denied entry, provided they can sufficiently show other proof that they are a bona fide student (e.g., a certificate of registration or another valid document).

Similar accommodation applies to uniform policy violations at campuses or colleges that require uniforms - proof of enrollment should still allow entry even without full compliance, though the student may still be referred for appropriate guidance regarding the policy.

Examinations and Delinquent Fees

Students with unpaid or delinquent fees still retain the right to take their examinations. This protects students from being barred from an exam purely over a financial matter. That said, the university retains the right to withhold other services or documents (such as release of grades, certificates, or clearance) until outstanding obligations are settled, depending on specific finance office rules in effect for the term.

Student Rights and Freedom from Militarization

PUP's student handbook affirms that the pursuit of academic excellence and the exercise of academic freedom can only be achieved in an atmosphere free from fear and unreasonable restraint. In line with this, no military detachment or personnel may be installed inside the campus, except for the university's Reserve Officers' Training Corps (ROTC) program, which operates under its own separate regulatory framework.

This provision is part of a broader set of student rights recognized in the handbook, meant to protect the university as a space for open academic inquiry.

Curfew and Overnight Stay Rules

For students residing in or making use of on-campus facilities, a curfew of 10:00 PM is generally in effect. Any overnight stay on campus beyond this curfew requires prior approval from the appropriate university office (such as the college dean, student affairs office, or dormitory administration, depending on the campus). Students planning group activities, org meetings, or academic work that may run late should secure the necessary permissions in advance to avoid being in violation of this policy.

Student Conduct and Code of Behavior

As representatives of the university, PUP students are expected to uphold high standards of behavior both on and off campus. Students are expected to know and respect the university's philosophy, vision, mission, and core values, which emphasize developing well-rounded citizens and leaders through quality, accessible education.

Violations of the student code of conduct are handled through the appropriate disciplinary process, typically involving the Office of Student Affairs (OSA) and, where applicable, the Student Council's own disciplinary or tribunal bodies.

PUP Student Council

The PUP Student Council (PUP SC) is the official representative body of the student population, mandated to organize and lead campaigns and activities that promote and defend students' rights and general welfare, and to provide direct services to the student body. The Council is composed of the Central Student Council (also known as the Sentral na Konseho ng Mag-aaral or SKM), local student councils in each college (including the Open University System and Institute of Technology), and independent bodies covering audit, elections, accreditation of student organizations, and a student tribunal.

Elections for student council positions follow a first-past-the-post voting system, with officers serving a term of one academic year. Students can get involved by voting in scheduled elections, joining accredited student organizations, or running for a council seat when nominations open.

Joining and Forming Student Organizations

Recognized student organizations at PUP must go through an accreditation process facilitated by the Student Council Commission on Student Organizations and Accreditation (SC-COSOA), in coordination with the Office of Student Affairs. Accreditation typically requires submission of a constitution and by-laws, a list of officers and members, and an adviser from the faculty, among other requirements set for each academic year.

Students who want to join an existing organization can approach the org directly during recruitment periods (often at the start of a semester), while those who want to start a new organization should coordinate early with OSA and SC-COSOA, since the accreditation process can take time.

Graduation Requirements

To graduate, a student must complete all required units and subjects prescribed in their program's curriculum, meet the minimum academic standing required by their college, and settle all outstanding financial and clearance obligations (library, laboratory, department, etc.). Most programs also require an on-the-job training/practicum component and, depending on the program, a thesis, capstone project, or comprehensive exam.

Students nearing graduation should coordinate early with their department and the Registrar's Office to verify their curriculum checklist and confirm there are no missing requirements, since discrepancies discovered late can delay graduation and clearance for the commencement exercise.

On-the-Job Training (OJT) / Practicum

Most undergraduate programs at PUP require students to complete an On-the-Job Training or practicum period, giving them hands-on industry experience relevant to their field before graduation. Requirements typically include securing an accredited or approved host company/organization, completing a minimum number of training hours, and submitting required documentation (such as a training plan, evaluation from the host supervisor, and a narrative report) to the OJT coordinator of their department.

Students are advised to start coordinating with their OJT/practicum coordinator at least a semester in advance, since host company placement, endorsement letters, and required clearances can take time to process.

Tuition and Miscellaneous Fees

As a state university, PUP offers heavily subsidized tuition compared to private institutions, with many programs falling under free or reduced tuition schemes for qualified Filipino students under applicable national legislation (e.g., free tuition laws for state universities and colleges). Students are still generally responsible for certain miscellaneous and laboratory fees, which vary depending on the program and specific course requirements (e.g., laboratory-heavy programs in engineering, science, or computing may carry additional fees).

Payment deadlines are tied to the enrollment period each semester, and students with unresolved balances may face holds on services such as release of grades or clearance, even though (per examination policy) they cannot be barred from taking their exams over unpaid fees alone.

Dropping a Subject or Withdrawing from the University

A student who wants to drop a subject must file the appropriate request through their department, to be submitted to the Registrar's Office for processing, generally before a set cutoff date each semester (dropping after this date without approval may instead result in a failing grade). A Withdrawn (W) mark is used specifically when the student formally withdraws in writing, and this request must be filed no less than one month before the final examination period for that subject.

Withdrawing from the university entirely (a leave of absence or full withdrawal) follows a separate clearance process involving the college, the Registrar, and other offices depending on the student's obligations at the time.

Shifting Programs and Transferring Campuses

Students who wish to shift from one degree program to another, or transfer from one PUP campus to another, must coordinate with the receiving college's Dean's Office and the Office of Admission Services. Requirements commonly include a minimum GWA, availability of slots in the target program, and completion of any bridging or deficiency subjects required to align the student's academic record with the new program's curriculum.

Shifting and transfer requests are typically processed within specific windows each academic year (often before the start of a new semester), so students are advised to inquire with their target college well ahead of the enrollment period.

Library Services and Clearance

PUP libraries (main and campus-level) provide students access to physical collections, reserved course materials, and in many cases online/digital resources and research databases. Students are generally required to present a valid ID and settle any outstanding library obligations, such as unreturned books or unpaid fines, before requesting graduation or transfer clearance.

Library hours, borrowing limits, and available digital resources vary by campus and are announced through the library's own official channels at the start of each academic year.

Open University System (OUS) and Institute of Technology (iTech)

Beyond its traditional resident colleges, PUP also operates an Open University System (OUS) that offers flexible, distance, and blended learning programs for students who are unable to attend regular on-campus classes - for example, working students or those in different regions. The Institute of Technology (iTech) similarly offers a distinct track of technology-focused programs.

Both OUS and iTech maintain their own local student councils under the overall PUP Student Council structure, and while their delivery mode differs from the traditional resident program, they generally follow the same core university policies on grading, attendance-equivalent requirements, and academic standing, adapted to their respective learning formats.

Guidance, Counseling and Testing Services (GCTSO)

The Guidance, Counseling and Testing Services Office (GCTSO) supports students through counseling services, testing (such as psychological or aptitude assessments used in some admission and section-grouping processes), and issuance of official excuse slips for absences related to documented personal or medical circumstances.

Students experiencing academic stress, personal difficulties, or who simply want guidance on academic and career planning are encouraged to reach out to GCTSO, which is generally available through their college or campus's student affairs unit.
